options.D: Run the eval suite automatically in CI on every prompt or model change and block merges that fall below the threshold

questions.explanationCorrect: Wiring the eval suite into CI so it runs on every prompt/model change and blocks sub-threshold merges makes the gate reliable and unskippable. Automate the acceptance check rather than relying on memory.
questions.explanationDistractor: Relying on engineers to remember manual runs (A) makes the gate optional in practice, so a rushed change ships unevaluated; automation removes the human-memory failure mode.

questions.stem: You want to set the confidence threshold above which actions auto-execute. On what should you base the threshold?

options.A: Measured performance on eval or held-out data at each confidence level, since raw self-reported confidence is often poorly calibrated
options.B: The model's own self-reported confidence number, taken at face value as the threshold for auto-execution
options.C: A round, easy-to-remember number chosen mainly for its simplicity rather than any measured evidence at all
options.D: Whatever single threshold ends up maximizing the overall share of actions that can be auto-executed without any human review at all in practice

questions.explanationCorrect: Thresholds should be set from measured outcomes at each confidence level on eval data, because models' self-reported confidence is frequently miscalibrated. Calibrate against ground truth, not the model's own number.
questions.explanationDistractor: Taking self-reported confidence at face value (B) can auto-execute wrong actions the model was overconfident about; you need the empirical relationship between stated confidence and actual correctness.

questions.stem: An auditor asks you to demonstrate that your model met its acceptance criteria at the last release. Which artifact best serves as evidence?

options.A: A verbal assurance from the team lead that the model did meet its acceptance criteria at the last release
options.B: A retained eval report tied to the specific model and prompt version, with the results and an accountable sign-off
options.C: The current production monitoring dashboard on its own, showing how the system happens to be behaving right now
options.D: The marketing announcement that went out to customers back when the release was originally shipped to them

questions.explanationCorrect: A retained, versioned eval report with results and a documented sign-off is the evidence artifact that proves the acceptance criteria were met at release. Evidence must be concrete, versioned, and attributable.
questions.explanationDistractor: The current production dashboard alone (C) shows present-day metrics, not that the specific past release passed its acceptance criteria; auditors need the retained record for that version.

questions.stem: Users report a class of failures your eval suite never covered. Beyond fixing the immediate bug, what closes the loop?

options.A: Add a quick note to the prompt about the failure and then otherwise simply move on to the next task
options.B: Wait to see whether users actually hit the same class of failure again before doing anything further about it
options.C: Add representative examples of the newly discovered failure to the eval suite so future changes are tested against it
options.D: Remove the feature that produced the failure so that this particular problem simply cannot recur going forward

questions.explanationCorrect: Turning discovered production failures into new eval cases prevents regressions and hardens the suite over time. The eval set should grow from real-world failures, not stay frozen.
questions.explanationDistractor: Only patching the prompt (A) fixes today's instance but leaves the suite blind to the failure class, so a future change can silently reintroduce it.

questions.stem: You have a promising new architecture that passed offline evals. How do you roll it out to production with the least risk?

options.A: Replace the old system with the new architecture everywhere, all at once, in a single simultaneous cutover
options.B: Ship it to every user on a Friday afternoon and then keep a loose eye on things over the weekend that follows
options.C: Keep the new architecture in staging indefinitely so that it never gets a chance to fail out in production
options.D: Roll out gradually (shadow or staged/canary), comparing live metrics against the baseline before expanding

questions.explanationCorrect: A staged or shadow rollout compares the new system against the baseline on real traffic and limits blast radius, so problems surface small. Offline evals gate entry; graduated rollout with monitoring de-risks the rest.
questions.explanationDistractor: Replacing everything at once (A) maximizes blast radius if the new architecture misbehaves on live inputs the offline evals didn't capture; graduated rollout contains that risk.

questions.stem: A compliance review finds several controls exist but no one is named responsible for operating and verifying them. Why is this a finding, and what fixes it?

options.A: Controls without an accountable owner tend to decay unnoticed; assign a named owner responsible for each control's operation and evidence
options.B: It is not really a genuine finding at all, so long as the code that implements each of the controls still exists somewhere in the repository
options.C: The fix is to add several more controls on top, so that coverage no longer depends on any single one of them
options.D: The fix is to drop the ownership requirement entirely so that the team has to carry less governance bureaucracy

questions.explanationCorrect: An unowned control drifts, breaks, or goes unverified because no one is accountable for it; naming an owner responsible for its operation and evidence is what keeps it effective. Ownership is part of the control, not overhead.
questions.explanationDistractor: Assuming existing control code is enough (B) ignores that controls need someone to operate, monitor, and produce evidence for them; code alone doesn't stay healthy on its own.

questions.stem: An eval rewards shorter answers, and the system learns to give terse, less-helpful responses that score well. What is the lesson for eval design?

options.A: Shorter answers are simply always better anyway, so the system learning to optimize purely for brevity is exactly the outcome that was wanted
options.B: Remove the eval entirely, since a metric that can be gamed like this provides no useful signal about quality at all to anyone whatsoever
options.C: The metric is a proxy being gamed; align the eval with the true objective (helpfulness and correctness), not an easily-gamed surrogate
options.D: Increase the model size, on the assumption that a stronger model will stop gaming the length-based scoring metric

questions.explanationCorrect: When a system optimizes a proxy metric at the expense of the real goal, the eval is measuring the wrong thing; align the metric with the true objective so improving the score means improving what you care about. Guard against proxy-gaming.
questions.explanationDistractor: Concluding shorter is always better (A) mistakes the flawed proxy for the goal — brevity was a surrogate for clarity, and optimizing it directly produced worse, terser answers.

questions.stem: Your routing sends too many cases to human reviewers, overwhelming them, while a stricter threshold would auto-approve some risky cases. How do you set the threshold responsibly?

options.A: Set the threshold to whatever clears the reviewer queue the fastest, regardless of the risk that doing so lets through
options.B: Choose the threshold using eval data to balance acceptable risk against reviewer capacity, and revisit it as data accrues
options.C: Eliminate human review from the flow altogether, so that the reviewer bottleneck simply disappears from the workflow
options.D: Route cases to reviewers at random so that the incoming review volume at least stays predictable from week to week

questions.explanationCorrect: The threshold is a risk/throughput trade-off best set from eval data — accept the quantified level of residual risk while keeping reviewer load sustainable, and recalibrate as more data arrives. Tune it on evidence, not convenience.
questions.explanationDistractor: Clearing the queue fastest regardless of risk (A) optimizes throughput while letting risky cases auto-approve — it ignores the cost-of-error side of the trade the threshold is meant to balance.

questions.stem: A regulator may later ask why the system made a specific automated decision about a customer. Which governance capability must be in place?

options.A: The ability to regenerate a fresh answer for the customer on demand whenever a past decision is later questioned
options.B: A standing guarantee that the model is always correct, so that no individual decision would ever need explaining
options.C: Only aggregate, month-level decision statistics for the whole system rather than any per-decision record of each specific individual decision itself
options.D: Traceability — a per-decision record of inputs, the model and prompt version, and the routing outcome, so any decision can be explained afterward

questions.explanationCorrect: Explainability after the fact requires per-decision traceability: the inputs, the model/prompt version, and the routing outcome recorded so any decision can be reconstructed and justified. Governance depends on this trail.
questions.explanationDistractor: Regenerating a fresh answer on demand (A) doesn't reproduce the original decision's basis — inputs, versions, and context may differ — so it can't explain what actually happened at the time.

questions.stem: In the first discovery session with a non-technical business unit, what should you focus on to scope the solution well?

options.A: Which specific model and context-window size you intend to build the whole solution on top of
options.B: The exact prompt wording you plan to write for the assistant, decided before anything else about the problem has been settled
options.C: The business outcome, success metrics, constraints, data sensitivity, and which actions must stay human-controlled
options.D: The cloud region and the specific compute instance types the deployment will eventually run on

questions.explanationCorrect: Effective discovery starts with the business outcome, how success is measured, constraints, data sensitivity, and which actions must remain human-controlled — these define the problem before any technology choice. Understand the need before the build.
questions.explanationDistractor: Leading with model and context-window choices (A) is premature — without the outcome and constraints you can't tell which model, architecture, or guardrails the problem even needs.

questions.stem: You must present three architectural options to non-technical executives so they can choose. Which framing is most useful to them?

options.A: Each option's cost, latency, accuracy, and risk implications in business terms, with a clear recommendation and its rationale
options.B: A deep technical comparison of token counts and raw API parameters across the three options for the executives
options.C: Only the single option that you personally happen to prefer, presented with none of the alternatives shown at all
options.D: A flat list of each option's features with no discussion of the trade-offs between cost, latency, accuracy, and risk

questions.explanationCorrect: Decision-makers need the trade-offs expressed in terms they act on — cost, latency, accuracy, risk — plus a recommendation and why. Translate architecture into business consequences.
questions.explanationDistractor: A deep dive on token counts and parameters (B) is unintelligible to non-technical executives and doesn't help them weigh the decision; frame it in business impact instead.

questions.stem: You are the only person who knows how the deployed system is configured and operated. Before you rotate off, what most ensures it survives your absence?

options.A: A single long email describing the entire configuration and how to operate it, written once and sent before you leave
options.B: Versioned documentation, runbooks for common operations and failures, and shared configuration in the repository
options.C: Keeping the operating knowledge in your own head and quietly staying available on call after you have rotated off
options.D: A screen recording of you talking through the whole system that the team can rewatch whenever they get stuck later

questions.explanationCorrect: A survivable handoff means the operating knowledge lives in versioned docs, runbooks, and shared config the team can find and use — not in one person's memory or a stale artifact. Institutionalize the knowledge.
questions.explanationDistractor: A one-time email (A) is quickly lost, unversioned, and can't be maintained as the system changes; durable runbooks and shared config in the repo stay current and discoverable.

questions.stem: You want every developer on a team to inherit the same standards, workflows, and tool configuration when they use Claude Code on a shared repo. Where do these belong?

options.A: Each developer's own personal ~/.claude directory, with the shared standards hand-copied one by one onto every individual developer's machine
options.B: A wiki page that every developer is asked to read through once during their initial onboarding week
options.C: Verbal onboarding walkthroughs that you personally give to each and every new hire who joins the team
options.D: Committed project files — CLAUDE.md for standards, .claude/skills for workflows, and .mcp.json with env-var expansion for shared tools

questions.explanationCorrect: Team-wide standards, workflows, and tool config belong in version-controlled project files — CLAUDE.md, .claude/skills, and .mcp.json with environment-variable expansion — so everyone gets them on clone and they stay in sync.
questions.explanationDistractor: Hand-copying into each personal ~/.claude (A) drifts immediately and misses new hires; committing to the project distributes and versions the setup automatically.

questions.stem: A new internal assistant is ready, and leadership wants org-wide adoption. Which rollout approach best manages risk and drives durable adoption?

options.A: A phased rollout starting with a pilot group, gathering feedback and fixing issues before expanding
options.B: An immediate, mandatory switch for all 5,000 employees on the very first day of the launch
options.C: A silent launch with no announcement, no communication, and no training offered to anyone at all
options.D: Leaving adoption entirely to chance, with no rollout plan and nobody driving it forward at all

questions.explanationCorrect: A phased rollout with a pilot surfaces real issues and builds advocates before scale, which manages risk and improves adoption. Learn small, then expand.
questions.explanationDistractor: A day-one mandatory switch for everyone (B) exposes the whole org to undiscovered issues at once and can sour adoption if early experiences are rough; piloting de-risks the expansion.

questions.stem: You are writing the operational runbook for the team that will support the system after handoff. Which content makes it most useful during an incident?

options.A: The system's marketing positioning and the pitch that was originally used to sell it to leadership
options.B: A complete history of every single design decision the team ever considered along the way to shipping
options.C: Common symptoms mapped to likely causes, remediation steps, rollback procedure, and escalation contacts
options.D: A verbatim copy of the model's full system prompt and nothing at all beyond that block of text

questions.explanationCorrect: An operational runbook is most useful when it maps symptoms to causes and gives concrete remediation, rollback, and escalation steps — what an on-call responder needs under pressure. Make it actionable for incidents.
questions.explanationDistractor: A full history of design decisions (B) is useful background but doesn't help someone resolve a live incident quickly; the runbook needs symptom-to-fix guidance.

questions.stem: Stakeholders are excited and assume the assistant will be right 100% of the time. What is the responsible way to set expectations?

options.A: Agree that the assistant is essentially perfect and effectively never wrong, so that the stakeholders' enthusiasm for the whole project keeps on running high
options.B: Communicate both the value and the limits honestly — including that outputs need verification for high-stakes cases — and describe the mitigations in place
options.C: Avoid mentioning any of the limitations whatsoever, so that nervous leadership does not decide to cut the project short
options.D: Claim the model never makes mistakes, on the grounds that you deployed the largest and most capable one available

questions.explanationCorrect: Responsible stakeholder communication states value and limits honestly, including where human verification is required, and the mitigations you've put in place. Overpromising erodes trust when reality lands.
questions.explanationDistractor: Claiming near-perfection to keep enthusiasm (A) sets stakeholders up for broken trust the first time the system is confidently wrong; honesty about limits is what sustains support.

questions.stem: Six months after launch, a new engineer questions why you chose a workflow over an agent and RAG over long-context. Which practice would have preserved that reasoning?

options.A: Relying on the original team's memory of why the workflow and the RAG choices were made at the time
options.B: Explanatory comments scattered across the codebase wherever the relevant components each happen to live
options.C: A single architecture diagram of the system with no accompanying narrative about why it looks the way it does
options.D: Architecture Decision Records that capture each significant choice, the alternatives considered, and the rationale

questions.explanationCorrect: Architecture Decision Records preserve the significant choices, the alternatives weighed, and why — so future maintainers understand the reasoning instead of guessing or re-litigating. Capture the 'why', not just the 'what'.
questions.explanationDistractor: Trusting team memory (A) fails as people rotate off and details fade; ADRs make the rationale durable and discoverable independent of who's still around.

questions.stem: A business unit brings ten possible AI use cases and wants them all now. How do you help them decide where to start?

options.A: Prioritize by business value against effort and feasibility and risk, starting with high-value, feasible, lower-risk cases
options.B: Start with whichever use case is the most technically difficult, in order to prove the team's engineering skill early
options.C: Build all ten of the requested use cases at the same time in parallel so that every stakeholder is satisfied at once
options.D: Pick whichever single use case the loudest and most insistent stakeholder in the room happens to want the most

questions.explanationCorrect: Prioritizing on value versus effort/feasibility and risk focuses limited capacity on the cases most likely to pay off soon and build momentum. Sequence by impact and feasibility, not by volume of requests or opinions.
questions.explanationDistractor: Building all ten in parallel (C) spreads the team thin and delays every outcome; disciplined prioritization delivers early wins that fund the rest.

questions.stem: A convention every engineer must follow — how the team wants tests written — is currently only in your personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Teammates aren't following it. Why, and what's the fix?

options.A: The convention itself is wrong and should simply be dropped rather than being shared any more widely across the wider engineering team
options.B: Personal user-level config isn't shared; move the team-wide guidance into the project's committed CLAUDE.md so everyone loads it
options.C: Teammates need to be reminded of the testing convention verbally each and every time that they start work, since nothing else enforces it
options.D: Put the convention into a Slack message and pin it to the team's channel so that people are always able to go refer back to it later

questions.explanationCorrect: User-level ~/.claude config applies only to you; team-wide standards must live in the project's committed CLAUDE.md so every teammate's session loads them automatically. Put shared guidance where it's shared.
questions.explanationDistractor: A pinned Slack message (D) isn't loaded into anyone's Claude Code session and depends on people remembering it; the project CLAUDE.md is applied automatically for everyone on the repo.

questions.stem: Your team performs a specific multi-step release-review workflow often, and you want Claude Code to follow it consistently when triggered, without loading it into every unrelated task. What is the idiomatic mechanism?

options.A: Paste the full release-review workflow into every prompt by hand whenever the team happens to need to run it
options.B: Put the entire release-review workflow into the always-on CLAUDE.md so that it gets loaded into the context for every single task the team runs
options.C: A project Skill (.claude/skills) with trigger keywords, committed to the repo so the whole team gets it and it loads on demand
options.D: Set up a personal shell alias on your own machine that runs the release-review steps for you when invoked

questions.explanationCorrect: A task/workflow like release review belongs in a committed project Skill that loads on demand via trigger keywords — reusable by the whole team without polluting unrelated tasks. Skills are for keyword-scoped workflows.
questions.explanationDistractor: Putting the workflow in always-on CLAUDE.md (B) loads it into every unrelated task, bloating context when it's only relevant during release review; Skills load on demand precisely to avoid that.

questions.stem: You are handing a production system to a new owning team. Beyond code and docs, what most enables them to safely evolve it?

options.A: Repository access to the production code, and nothing further at all beyond that handed to the new owning team
options.B: A standing personal promise that you will keep answering the new owning team's questions yourself for a full year
options.C: Only the exact prompt text that is currently running in production, without any of the surrounding tooling around it
options.D: The eval suite and monitoring dashboards, so they can validate changes against acceptance criteria and observe live health

questions.explanationCorrect: A team can only safely evolve a system if they can measure it: the eval suite lets them gate changes against acceptance criteria, and the dashboards let them watch live health. Hand over the means to verify, not just the code.
questions.explanationDistractor: Repository access alone (A) lets them change code but not tell whether a change is safe or whether production is healthy; the evals and monitoring are what make evolution safe.

questions.stem: An update will change how end users interact with an existing internal tool. What is essential for a smooth adoption?

options.A: Deploy the change silently and simply let the users discover the new interaction flow on their own over time
options.B: Communicate what's changing, why, and how to use the new flow ahead of the change, with support channels ready
options.C: Change everything all at once with no advance notice at all, on the theory that doing so maximizes the impact
options.D: Assume that users will read the release notes, even though in practice nobody actually publishes those notes

questions.explanationCorrect: Adoption goes smoothly when users know what's changing, why, and how to use it, with support available — change management is communication, not just deployment. Prepare the people, not only the system.
questions.explanationDistractor: Deploying silently (A) leaves users confused and frustrated, driving support load and resistance; proactive communication and support smooth the transition.

questions.stem: A non-technical product owner says they want 'accurate answers' and 'nothing risky.' How do you turn this into something buildable?

options.A: Work with them to define measurable acceptance criteria (what 'accurate' means and how it's tested) and classify the data sensitivity and prohibited actions
options.B: Accept the vague statement about wanting accurate answers and nothing at all risky exactly as-is, and then simply start building the feature without more questions
options.C: Tell the product owner that defining the requirements is really their own job to do, and not yours as the architect
options.D: Choose the largest available model so that accuracy is effectively guaranteed without ever defining it any further

questions.explanationCorrect: Vague goals must be converted into measurable acceptance criteria and explicit data-sensitivity and prohibited-action rules through structured questioning — that's what makes them testable and buildable. Turn intent into criteria.
questions.explanationDistractor: Starting to build on 'accurate' and 'nothing risky' (B) guarantees misalignment because neither term is defined or testable; you must operationalize them first.

questions.stem: The system is live. Leadership asks how you'll know it's delivering value and where to improve. What do you put in place?

options.A: Nothing further at all; shipping a successful launch is simply the natural end of the work on the project for the whole team involved
options.B: Only a simple running count of the total number of requests that the whole system ends up handling on each day following its public launch
options.C: A vanity metric, such as the raw parameter size of the model that you ended up deploying into production
options.D: Adoption and outcome metrics tied to the original success criteria, plus a feedback channel to capture issues and drive iteration

questions.explanationCorrect: Post-launch value is shown by adoption and outcome metrics tied to the success criteria you set, with a feedback loop that surfaces issues to fix. Measure against the goal and keep iterating.
questions.explanationDistractor: Treating launch as the finish line (A) forgoes the measurement and feedback needed to prove value and guide improvement; delivery continues after go-live.

questions.stem: A stakeholder worries the assistant might occasionally produce a confident but wrong answer. How do you address this constructively?

options.A: Deny that a confident but wrong answer can happen at all, in order to fully reassure the worried stakeholder
options.B: Tell the stakeholder that it is fundamentally a model problem which sits entirely outside of your own control
options.C: Explain the risk plainly and describe the mitigations — output screening, human review for high-stakes cases, and citations users can verify
options.D: Suggest that they should simply learn to trust the assistant's output rather than worrying about the occasional confident but wrong answer at all

questions.explanationCorrect: The constructive response names the real risk in plain terms and pairs it with concrete mitigations — output screening, human review where stakes are high, verifiable citations — so stakeholders see it's managed. Address limits with mitigations, honestly.
questions.explanationDistractor: Denying the risk (A) is dishonest and collapses when a confident error inevitably appears; naming it and showing the mitigations builds durable trust.

questions.stem: A teammate wants to personally customize a workflow that the project already ships as a Skill named 'deploy', without breaking the shared one for everyone. What is the clean approach?

options.A: Create a personal skill under a different name in ~/.claude/skills, because a same-named personal skill would shadow the shared project one
options.B: Edit the shared project 'deploy' skill directly so that it matches this one teammate's personal taste and preferred steps
options.C: Delete the shared project 'deploy' skill outright so that the teammate's own personal version becomes the only one left
options.D: Rename the shared project 'deploy' skill to something else so that only the teammate's personal variant stays active

questions.explanationCorrect: When skills share a name, Claude Code runs enterprise over personal and personal over project. A same-named personal 'deploy' would silently shadow the team's version for that user, so they would miss updates to it. A personal skill with a distinct name customizes privately without touching shared config.
questions.explanationDistractor: B changes shared team config to suit one person's preference, pushing the change on everyone who runs the workflow.

questions.stem: Adoption of a capable new tool is lagging because people don't know how to apply it to their work. What most effectively closes the gap?

options.A: Mandating usage of the new tool, with real penalties for anyone who is caught still not using it at work
options.B: Enablement — training, example workflows, internal champions, and office hours that show people how to apply it to their actual tasks
options.C: Removing the old tools that people currently rely on for their daily work so that they are effectively forced to switch over to the new one
options.D: Waiting silently for adoption to grow on its own, without any training, examples, or encouragement offered

questions.explanationCorrect: Lagging adoption from a skills gap is closed by enablement: hands-on training, concrete example workflows, internal champions, and office hours that connect the tool to people's real work. Enable people, don't just deploy tech.
questions.explanationDistractor: Mandating usage with penalties (A) breeds resentment and workarounds without teaching anyone how to get value; enablement addresses the actual cause, which is know-how.

questions.stem: At the end of a delivery phase, how do you confirm the solution actually meets what stakeholders agreed to?

options.A: Move automatically on to the next delivery phase as soon as the code has been merged in
options.B: Ask the engineering team whether they personally feel satisfied with what they ended up building
options.C: A formal acceptance review against the agreed criteria, with stakeholder sign-off recorded
options.D: Wait for user complaints to eventually come in as the signal that something did not meet the bar

questions.explanationCorrect: Confirming delivery means reviewing the solution against the previously-agreed acceptance criteria and recording stakeholder sign-off — an explicit gate, not an assumption. Tie acceptance back to the criteria you set.
questions.explanationDistractor: Asking only the engineering team (B) confirms it was built, not that it meets the stakeholders' agreed criteria; acceptance must involve the stakeholders and their criteria.

questions.stem: A client asks you to help them decide between building on the API versus adopting Claude Code for an engineering-productivity initiative. What is the most useful thing to deliver?

options.A: A neutral list of every single possible option laid out for them to read, with no guidance and no recommendation of any kind attached to it
options.B: Whatever option happens to be the newest one on the market, recommended regardless of their actual context
options.C: A decision deferred right back to the client to figure out on their own once they have thought about it more
options.D: A recommendation grounded in their goals and constraints, with the trade-offs that led to it and what would change the recommendation

questions.explanationCorrect: Clients are best served by a clear recommendation tied to their goals and constraints, the trade-offs behind it, and the conditions that would change it — decision-enabling, not just a menu. Advise, don't just enumerate.
questions.explanationDistractor: A neutral list with no guidance (A) leaves the client exactly where they started; your value as an architect is turning options into a defensible recommendation for their situation.

questions.stem: A team's first design for an employee benefits assistant is a five-step autonomous agent. The actual need is to answer questions from a benefits handbook, look up an employee's enrollment through one API, and remember the conversation. What should the architect propose as the starting point?

options.A: A multi-agent system in which a planner delegates handbook lookup and enrollment checks to two specialist subagents
options.B: An augmented LLM: a single model call equipped with retrieval over the handbook, one enrollment tool, and conversation memory
options.C: A fine-tuned model trained on the handbook so that it can answer benefits questions without any retrieval step at all
options.D: A fixed nightly batch that precomputes answers for every employee and serves them from a lookup table the next day

questions.explanationCorrect: The augmented LLM, a model enhanced with retrieval, tools, and memory, is the basic building block of agentic systems. When one call with those augmentations meets the need, start there and add workflow or agent structure only when the task demands it.
questions.explanationDistractor: A adds coordination cost and failure modes for a task that one augmented call already covers.

questions.stem: You are drawing the end-to-end architecture for a claims-summarization service: intake, a model call, and delivery to adjusters. The client wants quality to improve over time rather than stay frozen at launch. Which addition completes the design?

options.A: A larger context window on every call so that the model can see more of each claim file and needs no further tuning later
options.B: A quarterly manual review in which the team reads a random handful of summaries and adjusts the prompt from memory
options.C: A feedback loop that captures adjuster edits and ratings, feeds them into the eval set, and gates prompt changes on it
options.D: A second model call that rewrites each summary for style before delivery, so adjusters never need to edit anything

questions.explanationCorrect: An end-to-end design runs input, processing, output, and a feedback loop. Capturing real user corrections and ratings, turning them into eval cases, and gating changes on that suite is how quality compounds after launch instead of drifting.
questions.explanationDistractor: B is feedback in name only: a small, memory-driven review can't show whether a change helped or hurt.

questions.stem: A firm translates regulatory filings. There is a clear rubric for a good translation (terminology, register, no omissions), and reviewers find that a second pass guided by specific critique reliably improves the draft. Which workflow pattern fits best?

options.A: Evaluator-optimizer: one call drafts, another critiques against the rubric, and the loop repeats until the criteria are met
options.B: Routing: a classifier sends each filing to one of several translation prompts selected by the filing's document type
options.C: Parallelization: several independent translations run at once and the longest of them is kept as the final version
options.D: Orchestrator-workers: a lead model splits each filing into sections and hands every section to a separate worker

questions.explanationCorrect: Evaluator-optimizer fits when there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement adds measurable value: a generator produces a draft, an evaluator critiques it against the rubric, and the loop continues until it passes.
questions.explanationDistractor: D splits the work, but splitting alone doesn't apply the rubric-driven critique that improves quality here.

questions.stem: A migration assistant must update an internal API everywhere it is used. How many files and services need changes, and what each change looks like, only becomes clear after inspecting the codebase for each request. Which pattern handles this decomposition best?

options.A: Prompt chaining with a fixed sequence of five steps that is the same for every request, regardless of how large it is
options.B: Parallelization with a fixed set of four workers, each always assigned the same predefined slice of the codebase
options.C: A single call that receives the whole monorepo in context and emits every change at once in one large response
options.D: Orchestrator-workers: a lead model inspects the codebase, decides the subtasks at runtime, and delegates each one

questions.explanationCorrect: Orchestrator-workers suits complex tasks whose subtasks can't be predicted in advance: the orchestrator determines the pieces from the input, delegates them, and synthesizes the results. Parallelization needs its subtasks defined up front.
questions.explanationDistractor: B looks similar, but it fixes the split before anyone knows which files actually need changes.

questions.stem: A team is designing a multi-agent research system in which a lead agent spawns parallel subagents. Which TWO design choices follow sound orchestration practice? (Select 2.)

options.A: Give each subagent a clear objective, expected output format, and task boundaries so their work doesn't overlap
options.B: Have every subagent stream its full raw transcript back into the lead agent's context for maximum detail
options.C: Let subagents explore in their own context windows and return condensed findings to the lead agent
options.D: Spawn the same large number of subagents for every query so that coverage is always as broad as possible
options.E: Share one context window among all subagents so that each one sees every other subagent's intermediate steps

questions.explanationCorrect: Multi-agent systems pay off through context isolation: each subagent works in its own window and hands back a compressed result. Vague delegation causes duplicated or missed work, so the lead must give each subagent an objective, output format, and clear boundaries.
questions.explanationDistractor: D ignores cost: multi-agent systems use roughly 15 times the tokens of a chat, so effort should scale with query complexity.

questions.stem: A product team wants a multi-agent system to draft short sales follow-up emails, with a researcher, writer, and reviewer agent for each email. Volume is high and each email is worth little. What is the strongest architectural objection?

options.A: Multi-agent systems can't use tools, so the researcher agent would be unable to look anything up about the prospect
options.B: Multi-agent systems use far more tokens than single calls, a cost that low-value, tightly coupled tasks can't justify
options.C: Multi-agent systems require the Message Batches API, which cannot deliver the emails fast enough for this use case
options.D: Multi-agent systems only run on the largest model tier, which would make the per-email cost far higher than planned

questions.explanationCorrect: Anthropic reports that multi-agent systems use about 15 times the tokens of chat interactions, so they only make economic sense when the task's value is high and the work splits into broad, parallel pieces. A short, low-value email is a single-call or simple workflow job.
questions.explanationDistractor: D is false: model choice is per agent, and the real issue is total token volume, not a required tier.

questions.stem: A COO says the goal of a Claude deployment in the contact center is to 'cut average handle time by 20% this year.' Another executive wants to 'reinvent how customers get help.' How should the architect align the solution design to these goals?

options.A: Treat both goals as one, pick the most ambitious design, and measure success only by overall agent satisfaction scores
options.B: Ignore the business goals and optimize purely for model accuracy, since better accuracy eventually improves every metric
options.C: Separate an efficiency track with a measurable handle-time target from a transformation track with its own milestones
options.D: Defer any design until both executives agree on a single goal, since mixed value pillars can't be designed for together

questions.explanationCorrect: Efficiency and transformation are different value pillars with different designs and measures. Tie the efficiency work to a baseline and a measurable target such as handle time, and give the transformation work its own milestones, so each is judged on the value it is meant to deliver.
questions.explanationDistractor: B sounds rigorous, but accuracy is a means; without a business metric you can't show whether the deployment delivered value.

questions.stem: A team migrating a pipeline to Claude Opus 5.5 finds that requests setting temperature to 0 now fail, and a few simple extraction steps take longer than they want. What is the right adjustment?

options.A: Keep temperature at 0 but move it into the system prompt as an instruction, so the model reads it as a setting
options.B: Switch every step to extended thinking with a small budget_tokens value to cap how long the model deliberates
options.C: Remove the sampling parameters and lower output_config.effort on the simple steps, steering the rest through prompts
options.D: Prefill the assistant turn with the start of the expected output so the model finishes the extraction faster

questions.explanationCorrect: Sampling parameters such as temperature are removed on the newest models and return a 400, so steer behavior through prompting. Effort is the main control for how much Opus 5.5 thinks; lowering it on simple steps cuts latency and cost more reliably than prompt instructions do.
questions.explanationDistractor: B relies on budget_tokens extended thinking, which later models reject; current models use adaptive thinking with effort.

questions.stem: Incident summaries from a zero-shot prompt vary in structure and tone from run to run, and reviewers want them consistent. Which prompting change most directly fixes this?

options.A: Add three to five diverse example summaries in the target format, wrapped in example tags, to the prompt
options.B: Ask the model to be consistent in every response, repeating the request in capital letters for emphasis
options.C: Move the whole instruction into the user turn and remove the system prompt so the model has less to read
options.D: Send the same prompt three times and keep whichever summary happens to look closest to what reviewers want

questions.explanationCorrect: Few-shot (multishot) examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone, and structure. Anthropic recommends three to five relevant, diverse examples, wrapped in tags so the model can tell them apart from instructions.
questions.explanationDistractor: D spends three times the tokens and still leaves consistency to chance instead of fixing the prompt.

questions.stem: One step in a Claude Opus 5.5 workflow performs hard multi-step analysis of credit memos, and its answers are too shallow. Which TWO changes are supported ways to get deeper reasoning on that step? (Select 2.)

options.A: Raise output_config.effort to high or xhigh on the requests that run the hard analysis step
options.B: Apply a per-message effort change on just the hard turn, which avoids invalidating the prompt cache
options.C: Set thinking with a large budget_tokens value so the model has a fixed reasoning allowance each time
options.D: Raise temperature on that step so the model explores a wider range of reasoning paths before answering
options.E: Prefill the assistant turn with 'Let me think step by step' so the model begins with visible reasoning

questions.explanationCorrect: On Opus 5.5 thinking is always on and effort is the main control for how much the model thinks. Raising effort deepens reasoning; changing the top-level effort between requests invalidates the prompt cache, so a per-message effort change lets one turn think harder without that cost.
questions.explanationDistractor: C is the older extended-thinking control; budget_tokens is rejected on the newest models in favor of adaptive thinking and effort.

questions.stem: A finance agent needs detailed procedures for twelve tasks (reconciliations, accruals, audit requests), each several thousand tokens long. Only one or two apply to any request, and pasting all twelve into the system prompt is bloating context. Which reuse strategy fits best?

options.A: Keep all twelve procedures in the system prompt and add prompt caching, since cached tokens stop counting toward context
options.B: Split the procedures across twelve separate agents and route each request to the agent that owns the matching task
options.C: Summarize all twelve procedures into one short paragraph so that the system prompt stays within a small token budget
options.D: Package each procedure as an Agent Skill, so only short metadata loads up front and full instructions load when needed

questions.explanationCorrect: Agent Skills use progressive disclosure: roughly 100 tokens of name and description per Skill load at startup, the full instructions load only when a Skill is triggered, and bundled resources load as needed. Modular procedures stay reusable without occupying context on every request.
questions.explanationDistractor: A cuts cost and latency, but cached tokens still occupy the context window and still dilute attention.

questions.stem: An insurance quote assistant builds one long user message that mixes its rules, reference rate tables, and the customer's free-text request, and the model sometimes treats customer text as instructions. How should the prompt template be restructured?

options.A: Put all rules, rate tables, and the customer's text in one paragraph so the model reads everything with equal weight
options.B: Set the role and standing rules in the system prompt, and wrap reference data and customer input in separate XML tags
options.C: Remove the rules from the prompt entirely and rely on the model's default behavior to decide how quotes should work
options.D: Repeat the rules after every customer sentence so that no instruction can be overridden by anything the customer types

questions.explanationCorrect: A role and standing guardrails belong in the system prompt, and XML tags that separate instructions, reference context, and variable input help the model parse the prompt unambiguously and treat customer text as data. Templates with stable sections are also easier to test and cache.
questions.explanationDistractor: D inflates tokens and still leaves instructions and untrusted data mixed together without clear boundaries.

questions.stem: A RAG system over quarterly filings retrieves chunks such as 'Revenue grew 3% over the prior quarter' that don't say which company or quarter they describe, so answers attach figures to the wrong filing. Which indexing change addresses the root cause?

options.A: Shrink every chunk to a single sentence so each one carries exactly one fact and can't mix up figures from filings
options.B: Before indexing, prepend a short chunk-specific context (company, filing, period) to each chunk for embeddings and BM25
options.C: Raise the number of retrieved chunks from five to fifty so the right company is somewhere in the retrieved context
options.D: Replace retrieval by loading every filing into one prompt, since a 1M-token window can hold the full corpus

questions.explanationCorrect: The failure is chunks losing their context when split. Contextual Retrieval prepends a short, chunk-specific explanation before creating embeddings and the BM25 index; Anthropic reports it cuts failed retrievals by 49%, and by 67% when combined with reranking.
questions.explanationDistractor: A makes the problem worse: smaller chunks carry even less of the surrounding context that identifies the filing.

questions.stem: You are designing chunking and indexing for an HR policy library. Each policy has numbered sections, and older and newer versions of the same policy both stay in the repository. Which TWO choices make retrieval more accurate? (Select 2.)

options.A: Chunk along section boundaries and keep each section's heading path with its text
options.B: Store metadata such as policy name, version, and effective date so retrieval can filter
options.C: Index each whole policy as a single chunk so the model always sees the full document
options.D: Strip all headings before embedding so only body text influences the similarity score
options.E: Embed only the policy titles, since titles summarize what each document is about

questions.explanationCorrect: Chunking on the document's own structure keeps each chunk coherent, and carrying the heading path preserves context. Metadata such as version and effective date lets retrieval filter out superseded policies instead of hoping similarity alone picks the current one.
questions.explanationDistractor: C makes chunks too coarse: similarity is diluted across a whole document and the prompt fills with irrelevant sections.

questions.stem: Technicians search a knowledge base with queries such as 'E-4471 fault on model TX-900.' Embedding-only retrieval returns conceptually similar articles but often misses the one that contains the exact error code. Which retrieval strategy fits this query pattern?

options.A: Hybrid retrieval that combines BM25 exact-term matching with embeddings, merges results with rank fusion, and reranks
options.B: Switch to a larger embedding model and raise the similarity threshold so that only very close matches are returned
options.C: Drop retrieval and fine-tune a model on the knowledge base so it memorizes every error code and its fix article
options.D: Ask technicians to rephrase each query in plain language without codes so the embedding search matches better

questions.explanationCorrect: Embeddings capture meaning but can miss exact identifiers such as error codes and part numbers; BM25 excels at exact term matches. Combining both with rank fusion, then reranking, matches retrieval to a query pattern that mixes precise tokens with natural language.
questions.explanationDistractor: B still relies on semantic similarity alone, which is exactly what fails on rare exact tokens.

questions.stem: Executives ask questions such as 'What were total refunds by region last quarter?' The data lives in a governed SQL warehouse. A team proposes exporting the tables to text, chunking them, and using vector search. What is the better retrieval design?

options.A: Keep the vector search but add more chunks per query so that the aggregates are more likely to be fully covered
options.B: Paste a nightly CSV export of the warehouse into the prompt so the model can scan every row and add them up itself
options.C: Give the model a read-only query tool over the warehouse's semantic layer so it computes answers from live data
options.D: Precompute a summary paragraph for each table and let the model answer every question from those summaries

questions.explanationCorrect: Retrieval should match the data's shape. Aggregations over structured, governed tables are a query problem, not a similarity-search problem: a scoped, read-only query tool returns exact, current numbers and inherits the warehouse's access controls.
questions.explanationDistractor: B blows up context, goes stale overnight, and asks the model to do arithmetic over thousands of rows it could have queried.

questions.stem: An architect is choosing how Claude-based systems should connect to an internal ticketing platform. Which TWO situations favor exposing it through an MCP server rather than direct API calls in application code? (Select 2.)

options.A: The same ticketing actions must be usable from Claude Code, the Claude desktop app, and several custom agents
options.B: Several teams need one standard, discoverable interface with OAuth-based access instead of bespoke integrations
options.C: A single deterministic call with a fixed schema runs inside one batch job owned by one team and nothing else
options.D: A latency-critical code path already calls the REST endpoint directly and never needs the model to choose it
options.E: A partner's autonomous agent must negotiate and hand off whole tasks with your agent as a peer collaborator

questions.explanationCorrect: MCP is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data: build the server once and any MCP client can discover and use it, with standardized authorization. That pays off when many clients and teams need the same capability.
questions.explanationDistractor: E describes peer-to-peer delegation between agents, which is the job of an agent-to-agent protocol, not a tool connection.

questions.stem: A platform agent connects to twelve MCP servers exposing about 400 tools. Tool definitions consume tens of thousands of tokens before any work begins, and the agent increasingly picks the wrong tool. What is the most appropriate change?

options.A: Keep all 400 tools loaded and rewrite the system prompt to list every tool's purpose in more detail for the model
options.B: Split the agent into twelve agents, one per MCP server, and always run all twelve in parallel on each request
options.C: Use the tool search tool with defer_loading, keeping the few most-used tools loaded and discovering the rest on demand
options.D: Move to a model with a larger context window so that all 400 tool definitions fit with more room to spare

questions.explanationCorrect: Tool search provides progressive discovery: deferred tools stay out of context until Claude searches for them, and typically only three to five load per request. Anthropic reports it cuts definition tokens by over 85% and keeps selection accurate beyond the 30–50 tool range where accuracy degrades.
questions.explanationDistractor: D solves the token count but not selection accuracy, which degrades with the number of tools visible at once.

questions.stem: An expense-approval agent has six small tools, and every request uses nearly all of them. A developer proposes adding tool search with deferred loading because 'it is the modern best practice.' What should the architect advise?

options.A: Adopt tool search, because deferring every tool definition always lowers cost regardless of how many tools exist
options.B: Keep the six tools loaded up front; with few tools used on every request, on-demand discovery adds work without benefit
options.C: Adopt tool search and defer all six tools, so the agent has to search for each one on every request it handles
options.D: Replace the six tools with one generic tool that accepts free-text commands, so there's nothing left to discover

questions.explanationCorrect: Progressive discovery is a trade-off. Anthropic's guidance favors standard tool calling when there are fewer than 10 tools, every tool is used in every request, or definitions are small; tool search pays off at 10 or more tools, 10K or more tokens of definitions, or growing libraries.
questions.explanationDistractor: C forces an extra search step for tools the agent needs every time, adding latency and tokens.

questions.stem: An agent was given every endpoint of an internal API as its own tool: search_docs, find_docs, lookup_doc, get_doc, fetch_doc_body, and 35 more. It often calls near-duplicate tools and chains many low-level calls. Which change best addresses the capability bloat?

options.A: Add more detail to each of the 40 tool descriptions so the model can finally tell the overlapping tools apart
options.B: Keep all 40 tools and add a rule to the system prompt telling the model to prefer the first tool that works
options.C: Give the agent a single raw HTTP tool so it can call any endpoint of the internal API directly and flexibly
options.D: Consolidate overlapping tools into a few task-level tools with clear, namespaced names that return useful results

questions.explanationCorrect: Too many overlapping tools distract the agent and waste context. Build fewer, thoughtful tools that match real tasks, consolidating several low-level calls into one where it makes sense, with namespaced names and responses that return high-signal information.
questions.explanationDistractor: C removes the bloat but hands the agent unbounded capability, trading a selection problem for a security one.

questions.stem: A remote MCP server gives employees' Claude clients access to CRM records. It authenticates to the CRM with one shared service-account token, so any employee can retrieve records their own CRM role would not allow. What is the core fix?

options.A: Rotate the shared service-account token more often so that any leaked copy expires before it can be misused
options.B: Use per-user OAuth authorization so each request carries the employee's identity and the CRM enforces their access
options.C: Add a system prompt rule telling the model to only show records that belong to the employee who is asking
options.D: Log every CRM query the MCP server makes so that any inappropriate access can be spotted and reviewed later

questions.explanationCorrect: The gap is authorization, not authentication: a shared credential erases the user's identity, so the downstream system can't apply per-user permissions. MCP's authorization model is OAuth-based, letting the server act with the user's delegated access so the CRM enforces what that person may see.
questions.explanationDistractor: D is a detective control; it records the over-broad access but doesn't prevent it.

questions.stem: A live-chat assistant must show a first token within about one second, while a nightly compliance report built from the same data can take minutes and must be as accurate as possible. How should the configuration differ between the two paths?

options.A: Use one identical configuration for both paths so the results stay consistent and there is less for the team to maintain
options.B: Use the most capable model at max effort for both paths, since accuracy matters more than anything else in each case
options.C: Use the fastest, cheapest model for both paths, since latency and cost savings carry over to the nightly report too
options.D: Stream a faster model at lower effort for live chat, and run the report on a more capable model at higher effort

questions.explanationCorrect: Accuracy-latency trade-offs are set per path. Live chat needs streaming and a model and effort level that keep time-to-first-token low; the offline report can afford a more capable model and higher effort. Justify each choice against that path's requirement and verify it with an eval.
questions.explanationDistractor: A treats consistency as the goal and leaves one path either too slow or less accurate than it needs to be.

questions.stem: A team wants to A/B test a new support-reply prompt against the current one on live traffic before a full rollout. Which TWO practices make the result trustworthy? (Select 2.)

options.A: Randomly assign conversations to each variant and run both at the same time over the same period
options.B: Pre-register a primary metric and guardrail metrics, and a sample size, before the test starts
options.C: Run the new prompt this week and compare it with last week's results for the current prompt
options.D: Stop the test as soon as the new prompt pulls ahead, so users get the better version sooner
options.E: Let agents pick which variant to use for each conversation based on which one suits it best

questions.explanationCorrect: Concurrent random assignment removes time and selection effects, and deciding the primary metric, guardrails (such as escalation or safety rates), and sample size in advance prevents cherry-picking. Offline evals gate entry; a well-run live test confirms real-world impact.
questions.explanationDistractor: D is peeking: stopping at the first lead inflates false positives and often reverses at full scale.

questions.stem: A U.S. federal agency needs Claude for a workload that must run under a FedRAMP High authorization, with AWS as the sole data processor. Which deployment route does Anthropic's platform guidance point to?

options.A: The first-party Claude API with inference_geo set to "us", since U.S.-only inference satisfies FedRAMP High
options.B: Claude Platform on AWS, since billing through AWS Marketplace makes AWS the processor for inference data
options.C: Microsoft Foundry with a US Data Zone Standard deployment, since data zones confer FedRAMP authorization
options.D: Claude in Amazon Bedrock, which runs on AWS-controlled infrastructure with AWS as the operating party

questions.explanationCorrect: Anthropic's guidance says organizations that need FedRAMP High, IL4, IL5, or AWS as the sole data processor should use Claude in Amazon Bedrock, which runs entirely on AWS-controlled infrastructure. Compliance requirements choose the platform before any feature does.
questions.explanationDistractor: B is the trap: Claude Platform on AWS is billed through AWS, but Anthropic is the inference data processor.

questions.stem: An HR team wants Claude to pre-screen job applications and recommend who advances to interviews. Which TWO controls best address bias, fairness, and transparency? (Select 2.)

options.A: Evaluate recommendations across demographic slices for disparate error or selection rates before and after launch
options.B: Tell applicants AI assists screening, and route consequential decisions to accountable human reviewers
options.C: Rely on the model's general training to be neutral and skip fairness testing to save evaluation time
options.D: Hide the criteria and reasoning behind each recommendation so that applicants can't game the system
options.E: Train reviewers to accept the model's ranking by default so that decisions stay consistent across teams

questions.explanationCorrect: Fairness has to be measured: slice-level evaluation reveals disparate outcomes that averages hide. Transparency and accountability come from disclosing AI involvement and keeping consequential decisions with human reviewers who can explain and override them.
questions.explanationDistractor: E turns human review into a rubber stamp, removing the oversight the review step exists to provide.

questions.stem: During contracting, a client asks for a 99.99% availability SLA and 'sub-second answers' for a Claude-based assistant that depends on an external model provider and two internal systems. How should the architect respond?

options.A: Accept both targets as written to win the deal, and plan to renegotiate after launch if they turn out to be unreachable
options.B: Refuse to commit to any service levels, since model behavior makes every performance target inherently unpredictable
options.C: Promise the targets but exclude every dependency from the SLA, so that no outage ever counts against the commitment
options.D: Propose SLOs based on measured percentiles and dependencies, define what's measured, and document degraded modes

questions.explanationCorrect: Expectation alignment means grounding service levels in evidence: measured latency percentiles such as time-to-first-token, composite availability across dependencies, and explicit degraded behavior. Agree on definitions up front so everyone measures the same thing and the SLA can be defended.
questions.explanationDistractor: A wins the signature and loses the trust; unreachable SLAs guarantee a breach conversation later.

questions.stem: A platform team is rolling out Claude Code. They need (1) organization-wide guardrails, such as blocking reads of .env files, that individual developers cannot override, and (2) repository defaults that every clone picks up. Which TWO configurations meet these needs? (Select 2.)

options.A: Deploy the deny rules through managed settings, which take precedence over every other settings level
options.B: Commit a shared .claude/settings.json to each repository with its permissions and hooks for the team
options.C: Add a line to CLAUDE.md telling Claude never to read .env files, which Claude Code then enforces
options.D: Ask each developer to add the deny rules to their own ~/.claude/settings.json on their machine
options.E: Commit .claude/settings.local.json to the repository so every developer inherits the same rules

questions.explanationCorrect: Managed settings sit at the top of Claude Code's precedence order, so organization guardrails there can't be overridden, and deny rules are evaluated before ask and allow. A committed .claude/settings.json gives every clone the same project defaults.
questions.explanationDistractor: C shapes what Claude tries to do, but permission rules are enforced by Claude Code, not by instructions in CLAUDE.md.

cards.front: What are the four architecture options, simplest to most complex?
cards.back: Single call → workflow (code-controlled steps) → agent (open-ended, model-driven loop) → multi-agent. Pick the simplest that meets the requirement.

cards.front: When is a code-controlled workflow the right choice over an agent?
cards.back: When the steps and their order are known and fixed. Reserve agents for open-ended tasks whose path depends on intermediate results.

cards.front: When is an agent justified over a workflow?
cards.back: When the path isn't known in advance and the useful next step depends on what previous steps revealed (e.g., open-ended incident triage).

cards.front: When does multi-agent orchestration earn its overhead?
cards.back: Broad, separable work across independent areas that overflows a single context window, where parallel coverage matters more than token cost.

cards.front: Match the current Claude model to the task.
cards.back: Opus 5.5 is the default starting point for most workloads. Fable 5.1 for the most demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work. Sonnet 5.5 for the best speed/intelligence balance. Haiku 4.5 for fast, cheap, high-volume bounded tasks.

cards.front: RAG vs stuffing everything into a large context window?
cards.back: Retrieve only the relevant passages per query — cheaper, more current, and more accurate than loading a huge corpus every call, even with a very large context window.

cards.front: What is prompt caching best for, and how do you structure the prompt?
cards.back: A large, stable prefix reused across many calls; cache reads cost a fraction of full processing. Keep stable content first, volatile content last.

cards.front: What is compaction as a context strategy?
cards.back: Replacing older turns with a summary that preserves key decisions and facts, so a long-running session stays inside the context window. The Claude API offers server-side compaction (beta), so you don't write the summarizer yourself.

cards.front: Which entry point fits which user?
cards.back: claude.ai chat for ad-hoc; Projects for non-technical persistent instructions + knowledge; Claude Code for repo work; the API to build a product.

cards.front: How do you guarantee schema-valid JSON for a downstream system?
cards.back: Use structured outputs (output_config.format with a JSON schema) or strict tool use. Don't rely on prompt instructions, and don't use assistant prefill: it returns a 400 on the 4.6 family and later.

cards.front: First step when handed an ambiguous business ask?
cards.back: Scope it: clarify outcomes, volume, accuracy bar, data sensitivity, and which actions must stay human-approved — before choosing an architecture.

cards.front: Why stream long generations?
cards.back: Incremental tokens avoid request-level HTTP timeouts on long or high-max_tokens outputs. Assemble the full message from the stream when done.

cards.front: Correct handling of 429 (rate limit) and 529 (overloaded) responses?
cards.back: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, bounded attempts — never a tight immediate retry loop.

cards.front: How do you make a retried side-effecting tool call safe?
cards.back: Idempotency keys, so duplicate submissions of the same operation are deduplicated server-side. Don't just remove retries.

cards.front: Common silent prompt-cache killer?
cards.back: Volatile content in the prefix (datetime.now(), UUIDs, unsorted JSON, per-user tool sets). Any change to the prefix invalidates the cache after it.

cards.front: Which actions need human-in-the-loop before execution?
cards.back: High-impact, irreversible ones. Auto-approve cheap reversible actions under a threshold; gate the rest before they execute.

cards.front: What does a data-residency requirement constrain?
cards.back: Where inference and storage happen. On the Claude API, inference_geo offers only "global" or "us" (US-only is 1.1x price on 4.6+ models). EU-only processing points to EU-scoped endpoints on Bedrock or Vertex AI (10% premium). Encryption in transit alone doesn't satisfy residency.

cards.front: What must an auditable decision system log?
cards.back: Inputs, prompt and model version, tool calls, and outputs per decision — enough to reconstruct and defend any decision.

cards.front: Key model-layer observability signals in production?
cards.back: Token usage, latency percentiles, error and refusal rates, cache-hit rate, and live eval pass rate — not just host CPU/memory.

cards.front: Batches API — what fits and what doesn't?
cards.back: Fits large, latency-tolerant, non-interactive jobs (~50% cheaper, async, custom_id correlation, ≤24h). Does NOT fit interactive tool-calling loops — no mid-request tool execution.

cards.front: Where do production credentials belong?
cards.back: A secret manager or injected environment variables — never committed to source control.

cards.front: Graceful degradation when a data source is down?
cards.back: Return the available results and annotate the gaps or lower confidence. Don't fail hard, silently omit, or fabricate the missing data.

cards.front: Highest-impact cost lever for a large overnight non-interactive job?
cards.back: The Batches API (~50% cheaper). Prompt caching is a smaller, complementary saving, not a substitute for the batch discount.

cards.front: What are the three layers of the safety stack?
cards.back: Input screening, output screening, and tool-call authorization — defense in depth so one failure doesn't open the system.

cards.front: Fail closed vs fail open — which and when?
cards.back: Fail closed: on uncertainty or a failed check, deny or hold the action, especially for irreversible or high-stakes actions. The safe default is 'no'.

cards.front: Where should high-impact tool calls be authorized?
cards.back: In an external policy layer the system enforces before execution — not by the model's judgment or a prompt instruction. The model requests; the system authorizes.

cards.front: Core defense against prompt injection from tools or documents?
cards.back: Treat all tool/retrieved content as untrusted data that can't become privileged instructions, and enforce least privilege on the agent's tools.

cards.front: Why isn't a single system-prompt refusal instruction enough?
cards.back: It's a single point of failure; a jailbreak or injection that defeats it defeats everything. Layer independent controls instead.

cards.front: Best way to stop an over-powered tool from being misused?
cards.back: Replace it with a narrow tool that makes misuse impossible at the interface (least privilege) — better than a prompt telling the model to behave.

cards.front: PII data-minimization rule?
cards.back: If the task doesn't need the PII, redact or tokenize it before it reaches the model and before it is logged.

cards.front: Why not have the model judge whether its own input is a prompt injection?
cards.back: The attacker-controlled input can also manipulate the judgment. Enforcement must be external and deterministic, not in the channel the attacker controls.

cards.front: Why are BOTH input and output screening needed?
cards.back: Input screening can't see PII or unsafe content the model generates or pulls from tools at response time; output screening catches what leaves.

cards.front: How do you limit a 'confused deputy' agent?
cards.back: Least-privilege permissions plus a human gate on high-impact actions, so a hijacked agent can do very little.

cards.front: Guardrail for an irreversible bulk action?
cards.back: Require explicit human approval before execution. Logging after the fact can't undo it.

cards.front: How do you gain confidence that safety controls hold before launch?
cards.back: Red-team them — actively try to bypass the controls (jailbreaks, injection) before adversaries do.

cards.front: What role do evals play when changing a model or architecture?
cards.back: They are the acceptance gate. A change ships only if it holds or improves the eval scores; never ship a swap that regresses the eval set.

cards.front: What should acceptance criteria actually be?
cards.back: An eval set of representative inputs with graded expected outputs and a measurable pass threshold, defined before building.

cards.front: What three factors route a decision to a human?
cards.back: Confidence, reversibility, and cost of error. Irreversible, high-cost, or low-confidence actions go to a human; cheap reversible ones auto-proceed.

cards.front: In decision routing, what dominates even high confidence?
cards.back: Irreversibility and high cost of error — a confident but irreversible, high-cost action still routes to a human.

cards.front: Why not trust the model's self-reported confidence for thresholds?
cards.back: It's often poorly calibrated. Set thresholds from measured outcomes at each confidence level on eval/held-out data.

cards.front: How do you map a compliance obligation?
cards.back: To a named control that satisfies it, an accountable owner, and an evidence artifact (log, eval report, sign-off) that proves it operates.

cards.front: Why use a separate held-out test set?
cards.back: To detect overfitting — a prompt tuned against the same examples it's scored on inflates the score without real generalization.

cards.front: How do you grade open-ended output at scale?
cards.back: LLM-as-judge with an explicit rubric, run independently of the generator, validated against human labels.

cards.front: Why keep online monitoring after a strong offline eval?
cards.back: Live inputs and model/data drift can degrade quality after launch. You need both offline gates and online telemetry.

cards.front: A change raises the average score but regresses a critical slice — ship it?
cards.back: No — block it. Don't let an aggregate gain hide a regression on a safety-critical subset.

cards.front: How do you make the eval gate reliable?
cards.back: Run the suite automatically in CI on every prompt/model change and block merges that fall below the threshold.

cards.front: What evidence proves a past release met its acceptance criteria?
cards.back: A retained, versioned eval report tied to that model/prompt version, with results and an accountable sign-off.

cards.front: What should structured discovery focus on first?
cards.back: Business outcome, success metrics, constraints, data sensitivity, and which actions must stay human-controlled — not technology choices.

cards.front: How do you present architectural options to executives?
cards.back: In business terms — cost, latency, accuracy, risk — with a clear recommendation and its rationale, not a token-count deep dive.

cards.front: What makes a handoff survive your absence?
cards.back: Versioned docs, runbooks for common operations and failures, and shared config in the repo — plus the eval suite and dashboards — not one person's memory.

cards.front: Where do team-wide Claude Code standards, workflows, and tools live?
cards.back: Committed project files: CLAUDE.md (standards), .claude/skills (workflows), and .mcp.json with ${ENV} expansion (shared tools).

cards.front: Same-named skills in Claude Code: which one runs, and how do you customize privately?
cards.back: Enterprise beats personal, and personal beats project. A same-named personal skill silently shadows the team's project skill, so customize under a different name in ~/.claude/skills.

cards.front: CLAUDE.md — project vs user level?
cards.back: Team guidance goes in the committed project CLAUDE.md so everyone loads it; ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is personal-only.

cards.front: Best rollout approach for a new internal tool?
cards.back: Phased: start with a pilot group, gather feedback, fix issues, then expand. Communicate the change and provide support.

cards.front: What belongs in an operational runbook?
cards.back: Common symptoms → likely causes → remediation steps → rollback procedure → escalation contacts. Make it actionable under pressure.

cards.front: How do you set stakeholder expectations responsibly?
cards.back: Communicate value and limits honestly, including where human verification is required, plus the mitigations in place. Don't overpromise.

cards.front: What preserves the 'why' behind architecture choices?
cards.back: Architecture Decision Records capturing each significant choice, the alternatives considered, and the rationale.

cards.front: How do you prioritize a backlog of AI use cases?
cards.back: By business value against effort/feasibility and risk — start with high-value, feasible, lower-risk cases to build momentum.

cards.front: What is the augmented LLM?
cards.back: The basic building block of agentic systems: a model enhanced with retrieval, tools, and memory. Start here and add workflow or agent structure only when needed.

cards.front: Evaluator-optimizer vs orchestrator-workers: when is each the right fit?
cards.back: Evaluator-optimizer: clear criteria and iterative critique adds measurable value. Orchestrator-workers: subtasks can't be predicted in advance, so a lead model decides and delegates them at runtime.

cards.front: How much more do agents and multi-agent systems cost in tokens?
cards.back: Anthropic reports agents use about 4x the tokens of chat, and multi-agent systems about 15x. Reserve multi-agent for high-value, broad, parallelizable work.

cards.front: Temperature fails on a current model. What now?
cards.back: Sampling parameters (temperature/top_p/top_k) are removed on the newest models and return a 400. Steer with prompting, and use output_config.effort (low to max) to trade depth for latency and cost.

cards.front: How do Agent Skills keep context lean?
cards.back: Progressive disclosure: about 100 tokens of name and description per Skill load up front, full SKILL.md instructions load when triggered, and bundled files load only as needed.

cards.front: How many few-shot examples, and how should you format them?
cards.back: Three to five relevant, diverse examples, wrapped in tags (for example <example>) so they're kept apart from instructions and input.

cards.front: What is Contextual Retrieval?
cards.back: Prepend a short chunk-specific context to each chunk before embedding and BM25 indexing. Anthropic reports 49% fewer failed retrievals, and 67% with reranking.

cards.front: When do you add BM25 to embedding search?
cards.back: When queries contain exact identifiers (error codes, part numbers, names). Hybrid retrieval with rank fusion, then reranking, catches what semantic similarity misses.

cards.front: When should you use the tool search tool, and when should you skip it?
cards.back: Use it with 10+ tools, 10K+ tokens of definitions, multiple MCP servers, or a growing library (defer_loading on most tools). Skip it with fewer than 10 tools that every request uses.

cards.front: MCP vs direct API vs agent-to-agent: which is which?
cards.back: MCP: one standard server that many AI clients can discover and use. Direct API: a deterministic call inside your own code. Agent-to-agent: peer agents delegating whole tasks to each other.

cards.front: Why is a shared service-account token behind an MCP server an authorization gap?
cards.back: It erases user identity, so downstream systems can't enforce per-user permissions. Use OAuth-based delegated access so each call carries the user's authority.

cards.front: How do you fix capability bloat in an agent's toolset?
cards.back: Consolidate overlapping low-level tools into fewer task-level tools with clear, namespaced names and high-signal responses. Remove tools the role doesn't need.

cards.front: What makes an A/B test of a prompt change trustworthy?
cards.back: Concurrent random assignment, plus a primary metric, guardrail metrics, and sample size fixed in advance. Don't stop early the moment one variant pulls ahead.

cards.front: Which Claude features are unavailable on Microsoft Foundry?
cards.back: Among others: the Message Batches API, Models API, Admin API, and Managed Agents. Hosted-on-Azure deployments also exclude code execution, Agent Skills, and the Files API. Plan batch-discount strategies accordingly.

cards.front: What does HIPAA readiness on the Claude API require and exclude?
cards.back: A signed BAA plus a HIPAA-enabled org; only eligible features (most betas aren't) and non-eligible ones return a 400. Not available on Microsoft Foundry or Claude Platform on AWS, and Claude Code isn't covered.

cards.front: Which route does Anthropic point to for FedRAMP High, IL4/IL5, or AWS as sole processor?
cards.back: Claude in Amazon Bedrock, which runs on AWS-controlled infrastructure with AWS as the operating party.

cards.front: Two core controls for fairness and transparency in consequential decisions?
cards.back: Measure outcomes across demographic slices for disparate error or selection rates, and disclose AI involvement while keeping accountable humans on consequential decisions.

cards.front: Claude on Foundry: which data zone is available?
cards.back: Hosted-on-Azure Claude deployments offer Global Standard and a US Data Zone only. Hosted-on-Anthropic deployments are Global Standard and may process data outside Azure.

cards.front: How do you respond to an unrealistic SLA request?
cards.back: Propose SLOs grounded in measured percentiles (such as time-to-first-token) and composite availability across dependencies, define exactly what is measured, and document degraded modes.

cards.front: Claude Code settings precedence, highest first?
cards.back: Managed settings, then command-line arguments, then .claude/settings.local.json, then the shared .claude/settings.json, then ~/.claude/settings.json. Org guardrails go in managed settings.

cards.front: How are Claude Code permission rules evaluated?
cards.back: Deny, then ask, then allow; the first match in that order wins. A broad deny can't be carved out by a narrower allow. Rules are enforced by Claude Code, not by CLAUDE.md instructions.

cards.front: How do you monitor Claude Code usage and cost across a team?
cards.back: Enable telemetry (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1) and export OpenTelemetry metrics and logs to your observability backend with the OTEL_* exporter settings.
